beats.trigger: ## Evaluations
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The Module 5 eval now runs on every output.
beats.got: Something from a module I did not sit in is now running automatically; the rest is jargon so far.

beats.trigger: Start with the judge you saved at the close of Module 5.
beats.got: There is reading, and I am supposed to have a saved judge from before.

beats.trigger: **Build** a self-improving eval loop: separate agents generate and judge, the Module 5 judge scores each round unchanged
beats.got: One agent writes, another grades, and the grader never changes.

beats.trigger: Can agents improve if you define the outcome and let them find the path, or does organisational mess still matter too much?
beats.got: The question is fair. It is the one I would ask about any transformation: does the mess win?

beats.trigger: the system absorbs the catches without you.
beats.got: Work improves with nobody watching. Sounds nice, but I have heard it before.

beats.trigger: You can stay inside one loop. You cannot stay inside all of them.
beats.got: People cannot review everything, so you write down what good means and let a checker apply it.

beats.trigger: You saved the winner as `judges/groundedness-judge.md`: measured judgment, made runnable.
beats.got: A judge is a file with a standard in it that an agent can run. That is concrete enough.

beats.trigger: every name appears in the source, every number traces to a file, every claim cites evidence or admits the gap.
beats.got: The floor check is whether the facts trace to a source. That is useful and boring in the good sense.

beats.trigger: Groundedness protects the floor. Steering raises the ceiling.
beats.got: A second check for 'is it useful'. Floor and ceiling is neat phrasing, and I would like to see it work.

beats.trigger: If the judge moved, the score means nothing. If the generator improved under the same judge, the loop worked.
beats.got: The grader stays fixed and only the writer changes, so a rising score means something. I can check that with a file hash.

beats.trigger: The answer is never "the eval passed."
beats.got: Passing is not the same as being right. Fine, but it reads like a consultant's slide.

beats.trigger: A yardstick you rewrite is not a yardstick.
beats.got: Three rounds, 45 minutes, and I do something I can verify.

beats.trigger: Note what the judge catches; the tactic must learn that.
beats.got: I run it by hand once to see what it flags.

beats.trigger: Now step away. Come back to a tactic tightened by a judge you did not move.
beats.got: I leave, and a document is rewritten by the loop while I am gone. That is new compared to the last three programmes.

beats.trigger: If the judge file moved, the exercise failed; if only `./generation-tactic.md` moved, the loop worked.
beats.got: There is a pass/fail check I can run myself, and the page says what failure looks like.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: Each round's feedback went into the tactic file. A bit dramatic as a closing line.

beats.trigger: PDCA at the eval layer: Plan (generation tactic), Do (generate), Check (judge), Act (rewrite tactic).
beats.got: Plan-Do-Check-Act again. Yes, we had that one in the quality programme. Applied to agents it is at least runnable.

beats.trigger: Convergence was the floor in Module 5. Eval-as-yardstick is the ceiling here.
beats.got: I can reuse the loop with another judge. The floor and ceiling wording again.

beats.trigger: That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: Flagged claims fell to zero and the page says that is not proof of quality. Candid.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: A good score only shows the checker found nothing. It does not show the work is good.

beats.trigger: Nothing scores the judge.
beats.got: Score a handful of outputs myself and compare with the judge's verdicts. An afternoon of work, and I can test it myself.

beats.trigger: No release so far has told anyone what good means in your company.
beats.got: Better models make the fabrication check cheaper. Deciding what good means stays with me.

beats.trigger: The destination is not "the human disappears." You move one level up: you design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: Same message every programme gives: you move up to a more strategic role. Here at least the mechanism is concrete.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?
beats.got: A checklist of what must be in place before an agent sends an internal mail. It is a decent question.

beats.trigger: An ungrounded mail is a trust problem. A grounded but vague or tone-deaf mail is a usefulness problem.
beats.got: Nothing new. I already got this two slides ago.

beats.trigger: Variety in, selection out, memory keeps
beats.got: Generate many, pick the best, write down what survived. A slogan for something already explained.

beats.trigger: Some categories never go without a human.
beats.got: You decide per category whether the agent drafts, asks you first, or sends. Some things always stay with a person.

beats.trigger: Two judges now sit on disk: one keeps the work grounded, one steers it toward your standard.
beats.got: I write a second judge for my own idea of a good internal mail.

beats.trigger: Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops.
beats.got: The more reliable it gets, the less I look, and so the less I would notice it failing. That is true of every process I have owned.

beats.trigger: If the answer is a month, put one in your calendar.
beats.got: Read one output start to finish as the recipient would, on a schedule.

beats.trigger: Your role in the loop is to design the conditions under which the system earns more autonomy, one loop at a time.
beats.got: A summary diagram with the transformation vocabulary I have heard before.

beats.trigger: The judge file stays untouched: that's the integrity of the loop.
beats.got: Ask the agent to sharpen the tactic further, then review what it changed.

beats.trigger: If it sounds too kind, ask: *"Which rule did you claim to remove but keep under another name? Quote both lines."*
beats.got: The agent can flatter me, and there is a concrete question to catch it. Rare to see that said openly.

beats.trigger: The judge stays fixed and separate from the generator, so the score means something.
beats.got: Four points. Two of them I would repeat to someone else.

beats.trigger: Pick one call that should run through the eval loop before anyone relies on it, and write the trigger into your working notes.
beats.got: Homework: five agent calls, one of them to run through a loop.

beats.trigger: Trust the loop you can inspect.
beats.got: Trust what you can inspect. Sensible, and I would have liked it said earlier.

take_homes: The checker has to stay fixed and separate from the writer, or the score is meaningless. I can verify that with a file hash.
A flat or perfect score tells me about the checker, not the work. Nobody scores the checker unless I do, by comparing a handful of outputs against my own verdicts.
The cleaner it runs, the less I look, so I have to read real output now and then, as the recipient would.

monday.move: Nothing on the loop. Maybe take one report my team sends regularly, score ten of them myself, and see how far a hypothetical checker would agree with me.
monday.who: Me, with one analyst if it turns out to be worth it
monday.when: Not Monday. Possibly in two weeks, after the steering group.
monday.stop_condition: If scoring ten by hand shows nothing I would change, I drop it.
monday.blocker: Calendar full of the last programme's steering groups, and I have not seen the loop run on my own material.

misconception.why: The module said openly what the loop cannot do and gave me a check I can run myself. That is more than the earlier programmes offered. I still think much of this will fade as a fashion, but the verification part is a method rather than a slogan, so I would not call it a wait-and-see item.

one_line: First module this week that told me what it can't do and gave me a check I can run, but half the slides are still the same slogans in new clothes.
